title: Maryam bint Imran
subtitle: The only woman named in the Qur'an — chosen above the women of the worlds
sources: Qur'an 19 (Surah Maryam, entire)
Qur'an 3:42-51 — the annunciation
Qur'an 66:12 — 'and she believed in the words of her Lord'
Qur'an 21:91 — the spirit blown into her, her and her son a sign

chapters.heading: The Chosen One
chapters.body: When the angels announced Isa to her, they announced something else first: 'indeed Allah has chosen you and purified you and chosen you above the women of the worlds' (3:42). A young woman in the sanctuary of the House, dedicated to worship from childhood, guarding her chastity with such devotion that her guardian Zakariya found provision at her station out of season — 'It is from Allah' (3:37). When the command came, it came in the form of a visitor: a well-proportioned man. 'Indeed, I seek refuge in the Most Merciful from you, [so leave me], if you should be fearing of Allah' (19:18). He answered: I am only the messenger of your Lord, to announce to you a pure boy (19:19). She asked how a son could come to one untouched by any man, and the reply stands over history: 'Your Lord says: it is easy for Me, and We will make him a sign to the people and a mercy from Us. And it is a matter decreed' (19:21).

chapters.heading: The Palm Tree and the Child Who Spoke
chapters.body: The labor came upon her beside the trunk of a date palm, and her pain drove her to say — the Qur'an preserves it gently — 'I wish I had died before this and was in oblivion' (19:23). A voice called from below her feet: do not grieve; your Lord has provided a stream beneath you, and shake the trunk of the palm toward you; it will drop fresh, ripe dates upon you; so eat and drink and be contented (19:24-26). Provision descended at the moment of her greatest vulnerability — water and dates, exactly what a laboring mother needs. Then the greater miracle: her people accused her of a monstrous thing, and the infant in the cradle spoke by Allah's permission — 'Indeed, I am the servant of Allah. He has given me the scripture and made me a prophet, and He has made me blessed wherever I am' (19:30-31). Maryam's defense was her son's voice, and the Qur'an named its nineteenth surah for her — the only woman whose name titles a chapter, preserved for every generation of believers to recite until the end of time. And Allah Himself described her: 'and his mother was a supporter of truth' (5:75).

familyQuestion: Maryam was chosen 'above the women of the worlds.' What do you think made her so beloved to Allah — and what could you imitate starting today?

title: Asiya, Wife of Pharaoh
subtitle: The woman who defied the most feared tyrant on earth
sources: Qur'an 28:9 — '[He will be] a comfort of the eye for me and for you. Do not kill him'
Qur'an 66:11 — her prayer from inside Pharaoh's house
Qur'an 28:8-9 — the infant Musa brought to her

chapters.heading: The Tyrant's House, Allah's Refuge
chapters.body: The most dangerous address in the world at that time was Pharaoh's palace — and that is exactly where Allah sent the newborn Musa. His mother placed him in the river; the river delivered him to the house of the man slaughtering every Israelite son; and the woman of that house, Asiya, took the baby into her arms and said the sentence that crossed an empire: '[He will be] a comfort of the eye for me and for you. Do not kill him; perhaps he may benefit us, or we may adopt him as a son' (28:9). Pharaoh's own court ran on fear, yet in its heart this woman protected the very child whose existence Pharaoh had ordered erased. While her husband built towers and called himself lord, Asiya believed in the Lord of the worlds in secret — the Qur'an will call what happened next her greatest moment.

chapters.heading: The Prayer Allah Kept Forever
chapters.body: When Pharaoh's cruelty pressed on her — and when her faith became known — she made the dua the Qur'an carved into Surah At-Tahrim as a model for every believer: 'My Lord, build for me near You a house in Paradise, and save me from Pharaoh and his deeds, and save me from the wrongdoing people' (66:11). Look at the order of her prayer: nearness to Allah first, rescue second. Some commentators relate reports that Pharaoh tortured her for her faith and that she saw her home in Paradise and smiled; the Qur'an does not say how she died, and those reports were not opened for this audit. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ named Asiya, the wife of Pharaoh, with Maryam among the women who reached perfection (Sahih al-Bukhari 3411). A woman the world remembers only as 'Pharaoh's wife' — Allah remembers by her faith, and gave her what tyrants cannot touch.

familyQuestion: Asiya had everything a palace could offer and chose Allah instead. What would you hold onto if keeping it meant letting go of your faith?

title: Khadijah bint Khuwaylid
subtitle: Among the first to believe — the Prophet's ﷺ refuge and strength
sources: Sahih al-Bukhari 3 — the revelation and her response
Sahih al-Bukhari 3820 — Jibril's greeting to Khadijah and the promise of a house in Paradise
Sahih Muslim 2432 — Jibril tells the Prophet ﷺ to greet Khadijah and give her good news of a house in Paradise
Sahih al-Bukhari 3818 — Aisha's account of the Prophet's ﷺ remembrance of Khadijah and her friends
Seerah: Ibn Hisham, al-Sira al-Nabawiyya (ed. al-Saqqa et al.), vol. 1 pp. 188, 240 and 419 (Khadijah's wealth; her belief and support; the section on the deaths), read on shamela.ws, book 23833

chapters.heading: The First 'I Believe You'
chapters.body: When the angel came to Muhammad ﷺ in the cave of Hira and the weight of revelation began, he came home trembling and said: cover me, cover me. Khadijah held him and answered with the faith of a woman who knew his character well: 'Never! By Allah, Allah will never disgrace you. You keep good relations with your kin, you help the weak, you honor the guest, you bear the hardship of the road, you help against the calamities of truth' (Sahih al-Bukhari 3). Then she took him to her cousin Waraqa ibn Nawfal, who confirmed what had come to him. The seerah reports count her among the first to believe (the order of the first believers is discussed in the sources) — the one through whom Allah consoled His Messenger. Aisha said she never envied any of the Prophet's wives as she envied Khadijah, 'for he remembered her often' (Sahih al-Bukhari 3818).

chapters.heading: The Support He Returned To
chapters.body: Khadijah was a merchant of Quraysh in her own right, a woman of standing who hired men to trade with her wealth (Ibn Hisham, vol. 1 p. 188). Ibn Ishaq says she believed in him, trusted what came to him from Allah, supported him in his mission, and was the first to believe in Allah and His Messenger; Allah lightened his burden through her, so that he heard nothing that grieved him, of rejection or denial, but Allah eased it for him when he returned to her (p. 240). Ibn Hisham has a section on the deaths of Abu Talib and Khadijah, and says that after Abu Talib died Quraysh harmed the Prophet ﷺ more than before, so he went out to Ta'if (p. 419); the name 'Year of Sorrow' is not on the pages read. Aisha reported that whenever the Prophet ﷺ slaughtered a sheep he would say: send some to Khadijah's friends (Sahih al-Bukhari 3818). Years after her death, the household still honored her people.
chapters.label: Seerah report

familyQuestion: Khadijah's trust came from years of watching the Prophet's ﷺ character. Whose character do you know so well that you would believe them in a moment of fear?

title: Aisha bint Abi Bakr
subtitle: The Prophet's ﷺ beloved wife
sources: Sahih al-Bukhari 3895 — the Prophet ﷺ is shown Aisha twice in a dream before the marriage
Sahih al-Bukhari 4750 — the slander and her exoneration (the hadith quotes Qur'an 24:11-20 and 24:22)
Sahih al-Bukhari 304 — the Prophet's ﷺ words to the women on charity and the limits he saw (narrated by Abu Said al-Khudri)
Sahih al-Bukhari 3662 — asked which of the people he loved most, the Prophet ﷺ answered: Aisha (narrated by Amr ibn al-As)
Qur'an 33:6 — 'his wives are [in the position of] their mothers'

chapters.heading: The Girl Who Grew Up Beside Revelation
chapters.body: Aisha was the daughter of Abu Bakr and became the wife of the Prophet ﷺ. Before the marriage he told her that she had been shown to him twice in a dream: she was in a piece of silk, someone said, this is your wife, and when he uncovered it, it was Aisha; he said, if this is from Allah, it will be done (Sahih al-Bukhari 3895). Years later, on the return from a campaign, she was separated from the army and a slander was spread about her, led by Abdullah ibn Ubayy ibn Salul. She fell ill for about a month, the Prophet's manner toward her changed, and the Prophet ﷺ waited for revelation. Then her innocence was declared (Sahih al-Bukhari 4750, which quotes Qur'an 24:11-20 and 24:22). A passage of Surah An-Nur was sent down in defence of one woman's honour.

chapters.heading: Beloved of the Prophet ﷺ
chapters.body: In Sahih al-Bukhari 3662, Amr ibn al-As asked the Prophet ﷺ who was the most beloved person to him, and he answered: Aisha. The Qur'an says of the Prophet's ﷺ wives that they are 'in the position of' the believers' mothers (33:6) — Umm al-Mu'minin, the Mother of the Believers. The hadith literature also shows how he taught women directly: in Sahih al-Bukhari 304, narrated by Abu Said al-Khudri, the Prophet ﷺ addressed the women at the Eid prayer, urged them to give charity, and when they asked about his remark on deficiency in intellect and religion he explained it plainly, as a teacher to his students.

familyQuestion: Aisha asked questions even when the answer was hard. When was the last time you asked a sincere question about your faith instead of pretending to understand?

title: Fatima al-Zahra
subtitle: The leader of the women of Paradise
sources: Sahih al-Bukhari 3623-3624 — the leader of the women of Paradise
Sahih al-Bukhari 3714 — 'You are a piece of me'
Qur'an 33:33 — the Verse of Purification (Ahl al-Bayt)
Sahih Muslim 2450 — Fatimah wept, then laughed, on hearing she would be the first of his family to follow him

chapters.heading: A Piece of the Prophet ﷺ
chapters.body: Fatima was a daughter of the Prophet ﷺ, and he honored her: when she came to him, he would rise for her, seat her in his place, and honor her — and when he visited her, she would rise and seat him (Sunan Abi Dawud 5217 — sahih, al-Albani). To her he said: you are a piece of me (Sahih al-Bukhari 3714). The Prophet ﷺ drew his cloak over Fatima, Ali, Hasan and Husayn and recited: 'Allah intends only to remove from you the impurity, O people of the household, and to purify you with purification' (33:33) — the Verse of Purity, Ahl al-Bayt (Sahih Muslim 2424). The historians report her grief at the death of her father (source not checked here).

chapters.heading: The Inheritance of Dignity
chapters.body: When Fatima asked for a share of the Prophet's ﷺ estate after his passing, Abu Bakr answered her with his words: 'The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: we are not inherited from; what we leave is charity' (Sahih al-Bukhari 3092) — and she accepted it. The report adds that she was displeased with Abu Bakr over this; how to understand that is a question for scholars. In his last illness the Prophet ﷺ told her she would be the first of his family to follow him; she wept, then laughed (Sahih Muslim 2450). She lived months after her father, then followed him. Her legacy stands wherever the household of the Prophet ﷺ is loved: Hasan and Husayn, the leaders of the youth of Paradise (reported in the hadith literature). She is al-Zahra — the Radiant — and the Prophet ﷺ named her without hesitation: the leader of the women of Paradise (Sahih al-Bukhari 3624).

familyQuestion: The Prophet ﷺ called Fatima 'a piece of me.' What does it mean to carry someone's honor so carefully that you protect it like your own body?

title: Hafsa bint Umar
subtitle: The keeper of the sheets from which the Qur'an was copied
sources: Sahih al-Bukhari 4987 — Uthman has the Qur'an copied; the manuscripts kept with Hafsa
Sunan an-Nasa'i 3259 — Umar offers his daughter Hafsah in marriage; the Prophet ﷺ proposes (sahih — Darussalam)

chapters.heading: The Widow Who Became a Wife of the Prophet
chapters.body: Hafsa was widowed, and her father Umar — the second caliph — carried a father's worry for his widowed daughter. Umar had offered her in marriage to Abu Bakr and to Uthman, and then the Prophet ﷺ proposed to her (Sunan an-Nasa'i 3259 — sahih, Darussalam). She was known for her worship and her firmness; a woman of the household of revelation, with the strength of her father and the sensitivity of her faith.

chapters.heading: The Leaves in Her Keeping
chapters.body: After the calamity of Yamamah, when many who had memorized the Qur'an were martyred, Umar came to Abu Bakr with his famous warning: the death of the reciters is death for the Book — gather it. Abu Bakr hesitated — how could he do what the Messenger ﷺ had not done? — and Umar pressed until the leaves and scraps were gathered into a single book, and the sheets stayed with Abu Bakr, then Umar, then Hafsa (reported in Sahih al-Bukhari, Book of the Virtues of the Qur'an). When the copies were later standardized under Uthman, Uthman sent to Hafsa for the sheets kept with her, promising to return them (Sahih al-Bukhari 4987). Think of that: for a time, the sheets from which the Qur'an was copied were kept by a woman. When Muslims anywhere in the world open a mushaf today, its lineage passes through her house.

familyQuestion: Hafsa held the most precious book on earth and treated it as a trust, not a possession. What has been trusted to you that you are responsible for protecting?

title: Zaynab bint Jahsh
subtitle: Her marriage is spoken of in the Qur'an; her hands were known for giving
sources: Qur'an 33:37 — 'when Zayd had no longer any need for her, We married her to you'
Qur'an 33:28-29 — her choice answered by Allah Himself
Sahih Muslim 2452 — the longest hands; Zaynab worked with her hands and gave in charity

chapters.heading: A Marriage Heaven Arranged
chapters.body: Zaynab was the Prophet's ﷺ cousin, and it was Allah who arranged her marriage to his freedman Zayd — a union meant to erase the Arab distinction between freeborn and freed. The Qur'an states it plainly: 'there is no blame upon the Prophet in what Allah has decreed for him' — and when Zayd ended the marriage, Allah completed what He had ordained: 'when Zayd had no longer any need for her, We married her to you' (33:37). The chapter, Al-Ahzab, descended around the household of the Prophet ﷺ itself — the verse speaks of her marriage without naming her. What people might gossip about, Allah Himself narrated with honor.

chapters.heading: Generosity That Shook the Floor
chapters.body: Zaynab's name is tied in the hadith to her giving. Some of his wives asked which of them would be the first to join him; he said the one with the longest hands, and Aisha related that Zaynab's were the longest because she worked with her hands and gave in charity (Sahih Muslim 2452). When Allah offered the wives a choice — the glitter of this world, or Allah and His Messenger (33:28-29) — the wives chose Allah and His Messenger. History reports that she was the first of his wives to die after him (a history report; source not checked here).

familyQuestion: Zaynab worked with her own hands for the poor. What skill do you have that could become someone's provision?

title: Umm Salama
subtitle: The widow who said the dua of calamity — and whose counsel at Hudaybiyyah was followed
sources: Ibn Hisham, al-Sira al-Nabawiyya (ed. al-Saqqa, shamela.ws/book/23833), vol. 1 pp. 468-469 — the emigration of Abu Salama and Umm Salama, in her own account (read)
Sahih Muslim 918 — Umm Salama's dua when Abu Salama died, and the proposal
Sahih al-Bukhari 2731-2732 — Umm Salama's counsel at Hudaybiyyah
Jami' at-Tirmidhi 3211 (hasan per Darussalam) — the question about women and Qur'an 33:35; this report names Umm Umarah al-Ansariyya as the one who asked
Qur'an 33:35 — 'Indeed, the Muslim men and Muslim women...'

chapters.heading: The Wife Who Lost and Stayed
chapters.body: Umm Salama and her husband Abu Salama were among the early believers. When Abu Salama prepared to emigrate to Madinah, he set her on his camel with their son Salama in her lap and led the animal himself. Men of her own family, Banu al-Mughira, stopped them and seized her, saying he had overpowered them over his own person; his clan, Banu Abd al-Asad, objected, and the two sides pulled the boy between them until his arm was dislocated. Abu Salama went on to Madinah alone. For about a year she went out each morning to al-Abtah and wept, until a cousin of hers urged his clan to let her go and Banu Abd al-Asad gave back her son. She rode toward Madinah with only her son; at al-Tan'im Uthman ibn Talha asked who was with her, she said only Allah and her son, and he led her camel and escorted her, and she said she had never travelled with a more honourable man (Ibn Hisham, vol. 1 p. 469). Later, when Abu Salama died, she said the words the Prophet ﷺ taught for anyone struck by a calamity: that we belong to Allah and to Him we return, and asking Him to reward her in her affliction and give her something better. Allah replaced her loss: the Prophet ﷺ sent Hatib ibn Abi Balta'a to propose to her; she told him she had a daughter in her care and was a jealous person, and the Prophet ﷺ said he would pray about both (Sahih Muslim 918).
chapters.label: Seerah report

chapters.heading: One Question, One Verse
chapters.body: At the treaty of Hudaybiyyah, the Prophet ﷺ told the companions to get up, slaughter their sacrifices and shave their heads. He said it three times, and no one moved. He went in to Umm Salama and told her; she advised him to go out and say nothing to anyone until he had slaughtered his own sacrifice and called his barber to shave his head. He did exactly that, and when the companions saw it they got up, slaughtered their sacrifices and began shaving one another (Sahih al-Bukhari 2731-2732). Another report tells how a woman asked the Prophet ﷺ why the Qur'an addressed men and not women, and the verse came: 'Indeed, the Muslim men and Muslim women, the believing men and believing women ... for them Allah has prepared forgiveness and a great reward' (33:35). In Jami' at-Tirmidhi 3211 (hasan per Darussalam) the woman who asked is Umm Umarah al-Ansariyya, so this card does not attribute the question to Umm Salama. A woman's question became a verse — ask, and the sky can answer.

familyQuestion: Umm Salama said the words of the dua when her husband was taken from her, and her advice at Hudaybiyyah was followed. What do you say, and to whom do you turn, when something is taken from you?

title: Juwayriyya bint al-Harith
subtitle: The captive whose marriage is linked in the seerah to the freeing of her tribe’s captives
sources: Ibn Hisham, al-Sira al-Nabawiyya (ed. al-Saqqa, shamela.ws/book/23833), vol. 2 pp. 294-295 — Juwayriyya bint al-Harith and the captives of Banu al-Mustaliq (read; Not yet scholar-reviewed)

chapters.heading: The Thirst and the Answer
chapters.body: After the expedition against Banu al-Mustaliq, Juwayriyya, daughter of al-Harith ibn Abi Dirar, the chief of her people, was among the captives. She had fallen to Thabit ibn Qays ibn al-Shammas or to his cousin and had agreed with her master on a contract for her freedom. She came to the Prophet ﷺ, told him who she was and what had befallen her, and asked his help to pay it. He asked whether she wanted something better; he would pay her contract and marry her. She accepted, and he confirmed it (Ibn Hisham, vol. 2 p. 295, in Aisha's account). When the news spread that the Prophet ﷺ had married Juwayriyya, the people called them the in-laws of the Messenger and released the captives they held.
chapters.label: Seerah report

chapters.heading: A Captive Who Caught Barakah
chapters.body: In the same account Aisha says that because of this marriage a hundred households of Banu al-Mustaliq were freed, and that she knew of no woman who was a greater blessing to her people than Juwayriyya (Ibn Hisham, vol. 2 p. 295). As a reflection: honor given can return multiplied, and the strongest hand is the one that opens.
chapters.label: Seerah report

familyQuestion: One act of honor toward Juwayriyya freed a hundred families. What is one honorable act you could do this week whose ripple you may never fully see?

title: Umm Ayman (Barakah)
subtitle: The woman who cared for the Prophet ﷺ in his childhood
sources: Ibn Sa'd, al-Tabaqat al-Kubra (Dar Sader ed., shamela.ws/book/9351), vol. 1 p. 116 (Amina's death at al-Abwa; Umm Ayman brings him back) and vol. 8 pp. 223-226 (her biography) — read (not from the six books; Not yet scholar-reviewed)
Ibn Hisham, al-Sira al-Nabawiyya (ed. al-Saqqa, shamela.ws/book/23833), vol. 1 p. 168 — Amina's death at al-Abwa (read; this page does not mention Umm Ayman)

chapters.heading: The Mother After the Mother
chapters.body: When Amina, the Prophet's ﷺ mother, died, the boy was about six years old. Ibn Sa'd (vol. 1 p. 116) reports that Amina took him to visit his maternal relatives of Banu Adi ibn al-Najjar in Madinah, and that Umm Ayman went with them and looked after him; they stayed a month. On the way back to Makkah Amina died at al-Abwa and was buried there. Umm Ayman returned to Makkah with him on the same two camels; Ibn Sa'd says she had been his nurse alongside his mother and went on caring for him after Amina's death. Ibn Hisham (vol. 1 p. 168) also has Amina dying at al-Abwa on that return, but does not name Umm Ayman. In her own entry (vol. 8 pp. 223-225) Ibn Sa'd says the Prophet ﷺ inherited her from his father along with five camels and a flock of sheep, and freed her when he married Khadija. A narration there has him call her "O mother" and say, when he looked at her, that she was "the rest of my household". Her origin is not given in the pages read.
chapters.label: Seerah report

chapters.heading: At the Wounded on the Day of Uhud
chapters.body: Ibn Sa'd (vol. 8 p. 225), through Muhammad ibn Umar, says she was present at Uhud, where she gave water to the fighters and treated the wounded. The same author (vol. 8 pp. 223-224) says she married Ubayd ibn Zayd of Banu al-Harith ibn al-Khazraj, and they had a son, Ayman, who was a companion and was killed as a martyr at Hunayn; after the start of the prophethood the Prophet ﷺ married her to Zayd ibn Harithah, and she bore him Usama ibn Zayd. A narration there has the Prophet ﷺ say that whoever wished to marry a woman of Paradise should marry Umm Ayman. Her entry (vol. 8 p. 226) says she died at the beginning of Uthman's caliphate, and that she wept when the Prophet ﷺ died because revelation from heaven had stopped. All of these are Ibn Sa'd's reports, not hadith checked in the six books.
chapters.label: Seerah report

familyQuestion: Umm Ayman raised an orphan who became the best of creation. Who has cared for you when you had no one — and have you thanked them this year?

title: Sumayyah bint Khayyat
subtitle: A woman of Makkah who accepted nothing but Islam
sources: Ibn Hisham, al-Sira al-Nabawiyya (ed. al-Saqqa, shamela.ws/book/23833), vol. 1 pp. 317-320 — the torture of the weak among the Muslims and the family of Yasir (read; not from the six books; Not yet scholar-reviewed)
Qur'an 85:4-8 — 'companions of the trench [Containing] the fire full of fuel, When they were sitting near it' — cited as an illustration of persecuted believers; the verses do not name Sumayyah

chapters.heading: A Slave Who Refused to Move One Finger
chapters.body: Sumayyah is identified in the editors' note to Ibn Hisham as the daughter of Khayyat, a client of Abu Hudhayfa ibn al-Mughira. Banu Makhzum took out Ammar ibn Yasir, his father and his mother, a household of Islam, and when the midday heat grew fierce they tortured them on the scorching sand of Makkah. The Prophet ﷺ would pass by them and say, as Ibn Ishaq was told: be patient, family of Yasir — your appointed meeting is Paradise. Ibn Hisham says of Ammar's mother: they killed her, and she would accept nothing but Islam (vol. 1 p. 320). She was a woman with nothing left to take but her testimony, and on that she would not move. The Qur'an's chapter Al-Buruj (85:4-8) speaks of the people of the trench, who tortured believers for their faith while they sat near the fire; it does not name Sumayyah and is cited here only as a picture of persecution for faith. The sun that burned the sand of Makkah has long gone down. Her testimony is still on every tongue.
chapters.label: Seerah report

chapters.heading: The Family Yasir
chapters.body: What the Makkan torture could not understand was that it was building the thing it tried to destroy. A whole household — father, mother, son — out on the burning sand, and the Prophet ﷺ kept passing by with the same promise: patience, family of Yasir; your meeting-place is Paradise. Of the mother, Ibn Hisham says they killed her while she refused anything but Islam (vol. 1 p. 320). A note by the editors of the edition records that Ammar told the Prophet ﷺ that the torment had reached every limit; he answered, be patient, Abu al-Yaqzan, and prayed: O Allah, do not punish anyone of Ammar's family with the Fire (vol. 1 p. 319). Other details often told about this family — the fate of Yasir, the title 'first martyr', and the verse said to have come down about Ammar — are not in the pages read here and are not claimed.
chapters.label: Seerah report

familyQuestion: Sumayyah owned nothing but her faith, and she kept it at the cost of everything. What do you have that you would refuse to sell at any price?

title: Umm Ammarah (Nusaybah bint Ka'b)
subtitle: The woman who fought beside the Prophet ﷺ at Uhud
sources: Ibn Hisham, al-Sira al-Nabawiyya (ed. al-Saqqa, shamela.ws/book/23833), vol. 1 pp. 454, 466-467 (Aqabah) and vol. 2 pp. 81-82 (Uhud) — read (not from the six books)

Ibn Sa'd, al-Tabaqat al-Kubra (Dar Sader ed., shamela.ws/book/9351), vol. 8 p. 415 — her request and his ﷺ prayer for her family (read; given there without a chain on that page; not from the six books). The Musnad Ahmad attribution is not verified here.

chapters.heading: The Day the Men Broke and She Held
chapters.body: Nusaybah bint Ka'b — Umm Ammarah — of Banu Mazin ibn al-Najjar is named in Ibn Hisham among those who attended the second pledge of Aqabah, which he counts as seventy-three men and two women; the other woman was Umm Mani', Asma bint Amr of Banu Salama. The same page adds that Umm Ammarah took part in the fighting with the Messenger of Allah (vol. 1 pp. 454, 466-467). At Uhud, Umm Sa'd bint Sa'd ibn al-Rabi' asked her to tell what happened, and her account in Ibn Hisham runs: she went out at the start of the day with a waterskin to watch the fighting and reached the Prophet ﷺ while the Muslims were winning. When they were routed she moved to his side and fought, defending him with the sword and shooting arrows, until wounds reached her — a deep wound on her shoulder. She tells of Ibn Qami'a, who cried 'show me Muhammad': she and Mus'ab ibn Umayr and others who stood firm beside the Prophet ﷺ met him, and she struck him many times, but he wore two coats of mail (vol. 2 pp. 81-82).
chapters.label: Seerah report

chapters.heading: The Pledge, the Wounds, the Prayer
chapters.body: Ibn Sa'd (vol. 8 p. 415), in her entry under Banu al-Najjar, gives an Uhud report in her own words, with no chain shown on that page: the Prophet ﷺ told her to shoot; she hit the horse of a mounted polytheist in the eye with a stone, and rider and horse fell. The Prophet ﷺ watched and smiled, told her to bandage the wound on her shoulder, and said her station that day was better than that of certain men; he said the same of her husband. She then asked him to pray that she and her family be his companions in Paradise, and he said: "O Allah, make them my companions in Paradise." She replied that she did not mind whatever worldly harm had befallen her. On the same page Umar recalls the Prophet ﷺ saying that on the day of Uhud he saw her fighting in front of him wherever he looked. An attribution of this report to Musnad Ahmad is not verified here, and the wording above is Ibn Sa'd's. As a reflection: a mother's request answered by the Messenger of Allah ﷺ with a dua.
chapters.label: Seerah report

familyQuestion: When the Muslims were routed at Uhud, Umm Ammarah went to the Prophet's ﷺ side. What is the situation in your life right now that needs someone to go toward it instead of away?

title: Asma bint Abi Bakr
subtitle: The one with two belts — she brought food to the Prophet ﷺ and her father in the cave
sources: Ibn Hisham, al-Sira al-Nabawiyya (ed. al-Saqqa, shamela.ws/book/23833), vol. 1 pp. 486-488 — Asma, the food-bag and her waistband, Abu Jahl's slap, and Abu Quhafa (read; not from the six books; Not yet scholar-reviewed)
Sahih al-Bukhari 5224 — Asma in the early years of her marriage to az-Zubayr (carrying date stones)

chapters.heading: Two Belts, One Secret
chapters.body: While the Prophet ﷺ and her father Abu Bakr were in the cave, Asma bint Abi Bakr brought them their food-bag. She had forgotten to put a strap on it, and when they set off she could not hang it, so she untied her waistband and used it. Ibn Hisham says she was called Dhat an-Nitaq for this, and that he heard several scholars say Dhat an-Nitaqayn: she split her waistband in two, hung the bag with one half and wore the other (vol. 1 p. 486). When a group of Quraysh came to Abu Bakr's door and asked where her father was, she said she did not know, and Abu Jahl struck her cheek so hard that her earring fell off (vol. 1 p. 487). After Abu Bakr left, her blind grandfather Abu Quhafa came and said he must have left them with nothing, having taken his money with him. Asma put stones in the niche where the money had been kept, covered them with a cloth, and had him lay his hand on them; he said that if Abu Bakr had left them this, he had done well. The report adds that in fact Abu Bakr had left nothing and that she wanted to calm the old man (vol. 1 p. 488).
chapters.label: Seerah report

chapters.heading: The Girl Who Outgrew the Siege
chapters.body: Asma married az-Zubayr ibn al-Awwam. In Sahih al-Bukhari 5224 she describes the early years of the marriage: he had no property but a camel and a horse, and she did the housework, including carrying date stones from his land, which was about two miles away. Once the Prophet ﷺ offered to let her ride behind him, but she was shy before the men with him and thought of az-Zubayr's protective jealousy, so he went on; az-Zubayr later told her that her carrying the stones was harder for him than her riding with the Prophet ﷺ would have been. Later Abu Bakr sent her a servant to take over the care of the horse, and she felt as though she had been freed. The daughter who carried provisions to the cave also carried date stones for her household.

familyQuestion: Asma gave the Quraysh no help in finding her father, and took a slap for it. Has anyone ever trusted you with something hard to carry — and did you carry it?

title: Khawlah bint Tha'labah
subtitle: The woman whose plea Allah answered from above the seven heavens
sources: Qur'an 58:1-4 (Surah Al-Mujadilah, 'The Woman Who Argues') — revealed for her
Tafsir of Ibn Kathir on Al-Mujadilah

chapters.heading: One Sentence, Carried Above the Heavens
chapters.body: Khawlah's husband, Aws ibn As-Samit, in anger at her, pronounced the pre-Islamic formula of zihar — 'you are to me like the back of my mother' — a pre-Islamic formula by which a husband declared his wife forbidden to him like his mother. A woman in that position had no standing to object; the old custom had no court, no appeal, no voice. But Khawlah went to the Prophet ﷺ and argued her case — and she did not stop arguing. Ibn Kathir (on 58:1) records, from Aisha, the words of her complaint: 'He spent my wealth, exhausted my youth, and my womb bore abundantly for him. When I became old and unable to bear children, he pronounced zihar on me. O Allah, I complain to You' — and the revelation descended: 'Certainly has Allah heard the speech of the one who argues with you, [O Muhammad], concerning her husband and directs her complaint to Allah. And Allah hears your dialogue' (58:1). An entire surah is titled after her — Al-Mujadilah, the Woman Who Argues. From that day, the verses that followed gave zihar a ruling in Islam, and a woman's case had reached the sky itself.

chapters.heading: The Verse That Listened
chapters.body: What descended for Khawlah was not comfort — it was law. Those who pronounced zihar were told that their wives were not their mothers (58:2), that the formula was a monstrous word and a lie (58:2), and that the expiation was set in revelation itself: before they touched one another again, the one who made the declaration must free a slave, and if unable, fast two months, and if unable, feed sixty poor people (58:3-4). Her complaint became legislation — a family-law ruling arrived because one woman refused to accept injustice quietly. The same report names the husband as Aws ibn as-Samit, to whom the ruling applied. Khawlah's story stands in every generation's memory as the proof that in this deen, the unheard have a Listener — and that a woman's case, argued sincerely, can outweigh the customs of entire tribes.

familyQuestion: Khawlah argued her case to Allah and the sky answered. Is there an injustice in your life or community that deserves to be argued about rather than swallowed?

title: Safiyya bint Huyayy
subtitle: A captive of Khaybar — freed before her marriage, honored, not punished
sources: Ibn Hisham, al-Sira al-Nabawiyya (ed. al-Saqqa, shamela.ws/book/23833), vol. 2 p. 336 — the matter of Safiyya after al-Qamus (read; not from the six books; Not yet scholar-reviewed)
Sunan Abi Dawud 2998 — Safiyyah freed and married after Khaybar (sahih — al-Albani)
Sahih al-Bukhari 4200 — Safiyya among the captives of Khaybar; her freedom made her dowry
Jami' at-Tirmidhi 3892 — Safiyya taunted; 'Harun is my father, Musa my uncle, Muhammad my husband' (da'if per Darussalam)

chapters.heading: From Captive to Mother of the Believers
chapters.body: After Khaybar fell, Safiyya, daughter of Huyayy ibn Akhtab, was among the captives (Sahih al-Bukhari 4200). Ibn Hisham tells that when the Prophet ﷺ had taken al-Qamus, the fortress of Banu Abi al-Huqayq, Safiyya and another woman were brought to him; Bilal led them past men of their people who had been killed. The other woman screamed and threw dust on her head, and the Prophet ﷺ told them to take her away. He had Safiyya placed behind him and covered her with his cloak, and the Muslims understood that he had chosen her for himself. Ibn Ishaq was told that he asked Bilal whether mercy had gone from his heart, that he should take two women past their slain men (vol. 2 p. 336). Ibn Hisham adds that she had been the wife of Kinana ibn al-Rabi' and had dreamed that a moon fell into her lap; her husband struck her face so hard that it left a mark around her eye, and the mark was still there when she was brought to the Prophet ﷺ, who asked her about it. She had first been given to Dihya al-Kalbi. When a man told the Prophet ﷺ that she was the daughter of a chief of Qurayzah and Nadir and fit only for him, he had Dihya brought, looked at her, and told him to take another captive; then he freed Safiyya and married her (Sunan Abi Dawud 2998 — sahih, al-Albani). In Sahih al-Bukhari 4200 he made her freedom her dowry. A captive freed before her marriage and made one of the Mothers of the Believers — the pattern of this religion written in one life: a hard day that ends in honour.
chapters.label: Seerah report

chapters.heading: A Weak Report, Held Lightly
chapters.body: Jami' at-Tirmidhi 3892 (da'if per Darussalam) reports that Safiyya told the Prophet ﷺ that she had heard Hafsa and Aisha say that they were more honoured by the Messenger than she was, being his wives and his cousins. He told her what to answer: that they could not be better than her, for her husband was Muhammad, her father Harun and her uncle Musa. Because it is graded weak, it is mentioned with that caveat and no weight is placed on it. Later details of her life are not told here.

familyQuestion: Safiyya's freedom was made her dowry — she entered the Prophet's ﷺ household honored, not conquered. How do you treat people whose families were once against you?

title: The Queen Who Knew a Letter
subtitle: She ruled a kingdom, and a letter from Sulayman rearranged her throne

chapters.heading: A Letter With No Army Behind It
chapters.body: Sulayman's invitation to Saba came as paper, not soldiers: 'In the name of Allah, the Entirely Merciful, the Especially Merciful, Be not haughty with me but come to me in submission [as Muslims]' (27:30-31). No threat attached. The weight was entirely in whose name it opened — and the queen (named Bilqis in the tradition, not in the Qur'an), a sovereign who knew power, recognized a Power above sovereignty. She consulted her court: 'O my people, indeed I have been given a letter...'

chapters.heading: The Throne Moved Before She Did
chapters.body: Sulayman asked his court who would bring her throne, and a man who had knowledge of the Scripture brought it 'before your glance returns to you' (27:38-40). When Bilqis arrived and was asked, 'Is your throne like this?', she answered the question behind the question: '[It is] as though it was it' (27:42) — and she knew. Real power had met real Power, and she did not pretend otherwise.

chapters.heading: The Glass Floor
chapters.body: The final test was the gentlest and the deepest: a great palace whose floor was made of glass, laid over water. When she lifted her garment to wade, Sulayman said, 'Indeed, it is a palace [whose floor is] made smooth with glass' (27:44). What looked like an obstacle was solid ground. She said, 'My Lord, indeed I have wronged myself, and I submit with Solomon to Allah, Lord of the worlds' (27:44). The queen kept her crown and found her Lord — and became a woman whose submission the Qur'an records in her own words.

familyQuestion: What 'letter' — an invitation, a truth, a moment — has reached you recently that deserves an answer like Bilqis's?

title: She Ran Seven Times
subtitle: Between two hills, a mother in the desert ran history's most repeated search — and water rose
sources: Sahih al-Bukhari 3364 — the narration of Hajar and Zamzam
Qur'an 2:158 — Safa and Marwah are among the rites of Allah

chapters.heading: Left in a Valley With No Water
chapters.body: By divine command, Ibrahim left Hagar and the infant Ismail in the barren valley of Makkah and turned to go. The authenticated narration records her asking, 'Did Allah command you to leave us here?' He said yes. She said, 'Then He will not neglect us' (Bukhari 3364). A sentence of tawakkul standing in an empty desert — and on that sentence a whole rite of Hajj would one day be built.

chapters.heading: The Running Between the Hills
chapters.body: The water-skin emptied. The child cried. Hagar climbed Safa, searching the horizon; then descended and crossed to Marwa; then back again — seven crossings, the narration says, counting them as she went (Bukhari 3364). She was doing what every desperate parent does: exhausting every visible option while holding the invisible one. And 'He will not neglect us' held.

chapters.heading: Water Where the Heel Struck
chapters.body: At Marwah, she heard a voice — and the narration has an angel digging with his heel (or his wing) until water appeared, and she began to scoop it up, shaping it with her hands. The Prophet ﷺ said: May Allah have mercy on the mother of Ismail — had she left Zamzam (or: had she not scooped from it), it would have been a flowing spring (Bukhari 3364). Allah answered a run between two hills by writing it into the worship of every pilgrim until the end of time: 'Indeed, as-Safa and al-Marwah are among the symbols of Allah' (2:158). Every Hajj and Umrah repeats her search — and her finding.

familyQuestion: What 'empty valley' are you standing in right now — and what would 'He will not waste us' change about your next step?
